name: Colin Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Colin Abbott, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines since my certificate and apprenticeship. I know the railway-crossing equipment, though my pay is low for this trade; I use an approved AI assistant every day to sort repair photos, but I still put the meter and signed sheet first.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The basement pump failed and took almost all our savings. My partner Mina works part-time booking rooms and answering calls at a church office, and our grown children have households of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot the AI assistant saves me the last twenty minutes of note writing, but nobody should let it choose a live circuit. My hands still have to check the hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like trying new tools, yet our bank balance is too thin for comfort. My line pay is low, a basement pump failure took the savings, and Mina's part-time church-office hours depend on bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the scheduled repairs and use the approved AI assistant each evening to organize photos from the railway-crossing pole. In the first year Mina and I would stop the weekly café breakfast until the pump bill is gone; I'd check every generated circuit name against the signed sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel lively at the depot and tense when the pump invoice lands at home. Our grown children can visit for breakfast in our kitchen, but I won't ask them to fund it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the crossing pole?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train vibration loosened an old insulator, and the crack appeared only from the side. My AI photo label missed it until I turned the camera and checked the part myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep using the tool after that miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps sort the record, and I know what it failed to see. A second photograph and the inspection sheet fix the gap better than pretending a tool is perfect.

say: I'd credit **faster notes** after a late repair call at the depot.
I'd keep **live-circuit choices** with measured field checks.
think: The **pump failure** emptied savings while my line wage stays low.
Mina's **part-time office hours** add uncertainty to our household money.
do: Keep **scheduled repairs** and organize crossing-pole photos with the approved assistant.
Stop the **weekly café breakfast** until the pump bill clears; verify AI circuit names on the signed sheet.
feel: **Lively** at work, tense about the pump invoice.
S0.quote: My AI photo label missed it until I turned the camera and checked the part myself.
fieldNote: Colin's **daily AI use** includes a real missed insulator crack, which he corrected through a second angle and physical inspection.
The **pump bill** and variable office pay keep baseline anxiety high despite his enthusiasm for tools.

steps.text: Continue scheduled line repairs at the railway-crossing pole
Use the approved assistant to organize photos after field checks
Stop weekly café breakfasts until the basement-pump bill clears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our buyers and dispatchers to test any planning system with the crews before changing their shifts. A fast route and a wrong insulator make a very slow repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical work may continue for now, but Mina's office books room use and answers calls, which AI could take over soon. Dispatch might also tighten our overtime, leaving two small pay packets smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask to join the approved parts-order pilot and record every wrong match for old crossing hardware. In the first year Mina would ask for paid time to learn the new booking system, and we'd delay replacing our porch railing if either set of hours falls, while keeping it safe with a temporary repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel eager to test the parts tool and anxious about Mina's office hours. Our savings won't stretch through a long experiment with no pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part is easy to mismatch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older railway insulator takes a narrow pin that looks close to the new stock. I would log the pin size, not trust an image match alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the railing safely wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can brace it for now and keep people off that step. A full replacement can wait until we know the hours and can pay someone properly.

say: I'd seek **crew-tested ordering** before buyer and dispatcher shifts change.
I'd warn that **wrong insulators** turn quick routes into delays.
think: Mina's **booking and phone work** could shrink soon.
My **overtime** might also fall, leaving almost no reserve against two cuts.
do: Join the **parts-order pilot** and log wrong matches for crossing hardware.
Delay the **porch railing replacement** if hours fall; have Mina ask for paid booking training.
feel: **Eager** to test parts, anxious about Mina's wages.
S1.quote: A fast route and a wrong insulator make a very slow repair.
fieldNote: Colin recognizes **early thinking-work exposure** in Mina's bookings and phones, alongside possible cuts to his callouts.
His **parts pilot** tests a narrow pin measurement, and he plans a safe temporary porch brace before delaying replacement.

steps.text: Use the approved parts-order pilot and log wrong crossing-insulator matches
Brace the porch railing and delay full replacement if hours fall
Ask Mina’s office for paid booking-system training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI in 2028 could change Mina's office before robots reach my repairs around 2031. An employer should pay apprentices to test those machines, not just sell us courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 when capable robots arrive, I expect a major cut in line shifts. Mina's hours may already have fallen; we have less than a month saved and only a few line employers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the utility for its robot field-trial schedule and a paid equipment-testing apprenticeship. In 2029 I'd enroll if wages continue; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for posted testing or inspection work and use the community job board for openings in the next district.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wake up thinking how quickly two short payslips would empty the account. I'm ready to learn the machines. A willing learner still needs a paid place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the cracked railway insulator and ask whether the robot finds it from more than one camera angle. A dry-yard demonstration wouldn't show that fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a private course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the basement pump bill is still there. I need wages during training and a certificate employers actually recognise.

say: I'd separate **2028 office AI** from 2031 field robots when speaking to our crew.
I'd demand **paid testing apprenticeships** before crew cuts.
think: At **63**, I expect a major cut in line shifts.
Mina's **office income** may fall first while our savings cover less than a month.
do: Request the **robot trial schedule** and a paid apprenticeship now.
Enroll if **wages continue** in 2029, then seek posted testing work through the district job board.
feel: **Sleepless** over two likely smaller payslips, still ready to learn.
S2.quote: A willing learner still needs a paid place.
fieldNote: Colin expects **serious field-hour loss** after Mina's possible office cut and reports waking over household money.
His **trial request** uses a cracked insulator and multiple camera angles, while training depends on wages and recognised credentials.

steps.text: Request the utility robot field-trial schedule
Enroll in a paid equipment-testing apprenticeship in 2029 if offered
Apply for posted inspection and testing jobs in the next district

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell managers five years is plenty of time to test robots on real faults and make paid training available. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, then field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I might retire, but my lower wage and near-empty reserve don't prove I can. Mina's office work could change in 2031, so I need a household plan with a smaller second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd get my pension statement and join a paid robot trial if the utility invites experienced crews. In 2032 I'd take a funded inspection course with a real placement; when robots arrive in 2034 I'd compare the posted inspection wage with retirement income and keep paid line shifts until the numbers work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more room to move, but the pump bill still sits on the table. A longer runway helps me test equipment without pretending the rent has stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the trial report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd note whether the robot saw the crossing insulator crack from the side and how long a crew spent finishing the repair. The number of successful photos alone would flatter the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What income figure would you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mina's quiet-month pay, not her busiest booking month, plus my written pension estimate. We can only retire if that covers rent and medicine.

say: I'd ask for **real-fault robot trials** and paid training.
I'd mark **2031 thinking AI** and 2034 field robots as different dates.
think: Retirement at **66** remains unproved with lower wages and thin savings.
Mina's **office pay** may shrink before robots reach my repair work.
do: Get a **pension statement** and join a paid robot trial if invited.
Take a **funded inspection placement** in 2032 if offered; compare actual wages with retirement in 2034.
feel: **More room** to move, still pressed by the pump bill.
S3.quote: The number of successful photos alone would flatter the robot.
fieldNote: Colin's **2034 decision** compares real posted wages and a written pension under Mina's quiet-month income.
He proposes **failure-aware trial data**, including crew finishing time, rather than treating attractive robot images as proof.

steps.text: Compare written pension income with rent and Mina’s quiet-month pay
Take a funded inspection placement in 2032 if offered
Apply for posted inspection jobs in 2034 if retirement falls short
Keep paid line shifts until replacement wages or pension cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young lineworkers ten years is time to keep an honest record of the faults a camera misses. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to be retired before 71, but the pump debt and Mina's possible 2036 office cut leave that uncertain. I won't call my field job protected after 2039 simply because the date is distant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep taking paid repairs, clear the pump balance and request pension figures. In 2037 Mina and I would choose a retirement date only if the low-income budget covers rent; if it doesn't, I'd apply for a real equipment-inspection post before robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed by the robot clock and still uneasy about this month's bills. Ten years gives me room to learn, provided the pay continues while I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you rebuild a reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the pump balance is gone, I'd put twelve from each real weekend callout into savings. I won't plan on extra shifts that aren't on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fault record contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The railway insulator's stamped pin size, a side photograph and the measurement from the signed record. A trainee can check all three instead of taking a single AI label on faith.

say: I'd ask crews to record **camera-missed faults** over the decade.
I'd note **2039 robots** reach field repairs when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement before **71** depends on clearing pump debt and verifying pension income.
Mina's **office hours** could shrink in 2036, changing the household plan.
do: Keep **paid repairs**, clear pump debt and request pension figures.
Save **twelve from actual callouts** after debt clears, then test retirement in 2037.
feel: **Less pressed** by robots, uneasy about this month's bills.
S4.quote: A trainee can check all three instead of taking a single AI label on faith.
fieldNote: Colin's **long runway** still contains current pump debt and Mina's earlier office-work exposure.
His **fault record** combines part stamp, side photograph and signed measurement, while saving only follows debt clearance.

steps.text: Keep paid line repairs and clear the basement-pump balance
Save twelve from actual weekend callouts after debt clears
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if low-income figures cover rent
Apply for a real equipment-inspection post if pension income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Mina's office hours could fall before robots cut my field shifts in 2031. Paid equipment apprenticeships, honest robot trials, real job postings and a workable pension estimate would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the robot found the crack from the side or only passed the tidy front photograph. A successful image isn't the same as a safe line.

headlineQuote: A successful image isn't the same as a safe line.
portrait: Colin is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship, low pay and less than one month saved.
His **basement-pump debt** and Mina's part-time office income make even a mild AI outcome financially tense.
He uses **AI every day** to organize photos, yet checks unusual parts against physical marks, meters and signed records.
The **2031 robot date** alarms him because Mina's office work may shrink first and he expects major field-hour losses.
More warning offers **paid trials**, while he clears debt and keeps paid repairs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Colin most because Mina's office hours may fall before 2031 robots cut his field work.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **paid apprenticeships**, honest robot trials, actual job postings and a workable pension estimate.
